paras: The killing of Furgeson was the fatal shooting of a Black man at the railroad depot in Monroe, North Carolina, as he ran from H. J. Bivens, then constable of Monroe township, who was trying to arrest him for "beating a ride on the train." Bivens was tried for manslaughter in August 1905, and the trial ended in a mistrial when the jury failed to agree. The Monroe Journal called it the case "of most interest" in that term of court.

Furgeson, whose first name was not given, was accused of riding a train without paying. The date of the shooting does not appear in the coverage, which describes it only as taking place on a morning when an excursion crowd was at the depot.
When Bivens tried to arrest him, Furgeson ran, and Bivens fired at least four shots. Furgeson was struck by a pistol ball and killed.

Bivens was charged with manslaughter and tried in the court term that adjourned on a Friday night, apparently August 4, 1905. The jury received the case at 3 o'clock that afternoon, stayed out until 10:30, and failed to agree, and the judge ordered a mistrial. No report of a retrial was found.

The episode survives in a single item, a court column in the Monroe Journal of August 8, 1905, headed "Court Proceedings-Bivens Case Mistrial." The column stated without qualification that Bivens "shot and killed a negro," yet its account of the trial set out only the defence's evidence and gave no account of the prosecution's case. The item then moved on to a list of liquor, larceny and concealed-weapons cases from the same term.
No coverage of the shooting or the trial was found in other white papers or in the Black press.

Whether Bivens fired the fatal shot was the central question at trial. According to the Monroe Journal, the defence proved that his first two shots went into the ground, and Bivens swore that the other two did as well. The defence also offered proof that the fatal bullet and powder were not the kind Bivens used, and argued that an unknown bystander in the excursion crowd, hearing the shots and seeing the man run, had fired the fatal ball. This version came from the accused officer's side, and the jury did not resolve it.

reader.title: Killing of Furgeson at Monroe, North Carolina
bases: A constable of Monroe township fired at a Black man who ran when the constable tried to arrest him, and the man was killed; the constable was tried for manslaughter (A1).

The only report is one local court column (A1); it states Bivens shot and killed the man but also records the defence's proof that an unknown bystander fired the fatal ball, and the jury did not agree.

accounts.label: Monroe Journal court report
accounts.gist: Bivens, while constable, shot and killed a Black man who had been beating a ride on the train and ran when Bivens tried to arrest him.

accounts.label: Defence at trial
accounts.gist: Bivens fired his first two shots into the ground and swore the other two were too; the fatal bullet and powder were not the kind he used, and an unknown bystander in the excursion crowd, seeing the man run, may have fired the fatal shot.

framing.detail: The Monroe Journal headed its column "Court Proceedings-Bivens Case Mistrial," stated flatly that Bivens shot and killed the man, but gave space only to the defence's evidence that someone else fired.

versions.value: Bivens shot and killed Furgeson (the paper's own statement and the manslaughter charge)
The fatal ball was fired by an unknown bystander in the excursion crowd, not by Bivens (defence)

conflicts.note: Both versions are in the one report; the defence version is the officer's side, and the jury did not resolve the question.
